title: Who is in charge?
teaches: Agreement by majority (Paxos and Raft), leader leases, fencing tokens, and keeping the agreeing part small
summary: **Two servers monitoring each other cannot safely elect a leader.** When the network link between them fails, each server sees the other stop responding and promotes itself, resulting in split brain.
**Safe agreement requires a majority quorum.** Because any two majorities of the same group overlap by at least one server, two sides of a network partition cannot both reach a decision.

**A five-server group tolerates two failures; a three-server group tolerates one.** Committing a write requires a network round trip to a majority of servers, taking less than 1 ms within a datacentre and 30 to 70 ms across a continent.

**Raft maintains a replicated log managed by at most one leader per term.** A log entry is committed once the leader replicates it to a majority of servers, and voters only elect candidates whose logs are at least as up to date as their own.

**A partitioned minority cannot commit writes.** An isolated leader on the minority side of a split can append writes to its local log, but cannot commit them, and the cluster overwrites those uncommitted entries once the partition heals.
**A lease lets a leader act alone for a fixed time.** It must stop when the lease runs out, and nobody else may lead until it has.
**A paused process cannot detect that its lease has expired.** Storage systems must verify a monotonically increasing fencing token on every write and reject requests carrying older tokens.
**Restrict consensus to small metadata and infrequent updates.** Use a coordination service to elect leaders and store configuration, keeping consensus rounds off the high-throughput request path.

blocks.text: At 22:52 UTC on 21 October 2018, engineers replacing a failing piece of 100G optical network equipment at GitHub cut the link between its network hub on the US East Coast and its main East Coast datacentre. The link came back 43 seconds later. In those seconds GitHub's failover tooling, a system called Orchestrator that manages its MySQL databases, saw the East Coast primaries as unreachable and promoted replicas on the West Coast to take their place. Applications began writing to the West Coast databases. However, the East Coast primaries had accepted a few seconds of writes that had not yet reached the West Coast, because replication between them was asynchronous (lesson 4), and now the West Coast held writes the East Coast lacked.

Two sets of databases each held writes the other lacked, and no automatic process could merge them. GitHub chose to keep the site in a degraded state rather than lose data, and spent the next 24 hours and 11 minutes restoring backups, replaying writes and checking them. The engineers' post-incident report, published nine days later, explains how a valid failover decision still left them with two conflicting write histories.

We have deferred the question of how to elect a leader since lesson 4. GFS (lesson 6) and Bigtable (lesson 10) each have a single master, MapReduce (lesson 8) has a single master per job, and the databases in lesson 4 have a single primary. Each of those designs is simple only while every machine agrees on which server is the leader. When that server fails, or appears to fail, the system must choose a replacement, and every machine must reach the same decision even while network packets drop and clocks drift.

Consider a simple two-server design. A primary and a standby send each other a **heartbeat**, a small "I am alive" message, every second; if the standby hears nothing for ten seconds, it promotes itself. When the primary dies, this works. When the network between them fails and both stay up, each sees the other go silent, the standby promotes itself, the primary carries on, and two machines accept writes for the same data. This failure mode is called **split brain**, and no timeout duration prevents it, because from either side a dead machine and an unreachable machine are indistinguishable.

Google encountered this problem repeatedly. At the OSDI conference in Seattle in November 2006, where Google also presented Bigtable, Mike Burrows presented "The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems". Google's engineers needed leader election for the GFS master, the Bigtable master, and MapReduce's job masters, and each team that wrote its own implementation made subtle errors. Rather than distribute a software library for **consensus**, the problem of getting several machines to agree on one value even when some crash or disconnect, Burrows built a central network service that applications could call.

A Chubby **cell** consists of five servers, usually placed in different racks within one datacentre. To clients, it looks like a small file system of directories and small files, any of which can also be acquired as a lock. To become the GFS master, a server opens a designated file and requests its lock; the server that acquires the lock becomes the master and writes its network address into the file so clients can find it. Bigtable used Chubby to elect its master, to track active tablet servers (lesson 10) via per-server files, and to store the location of its root tablet. Engineers ended up using Chubby most heavily as a name service, storing small, rarely changed records that thousands of machines read.

To keep Chubby fast and reliable, Burrows kept the state requiring agreement small. A cell agrees only on changes to a few kilobytes of files and locks, at a rate of a few hundred operations a second at most, and its locks are **coarse**, held for hours or days rather than acquired for every request. The tens of thousands of clients connected to one cell mostly read cached copies of files, which the cell's master invalidates when the files change. High-volume traffic, such as GFS chunk transfers and Bigtable reads and writes, never passes through Chubby.

Inside a Chubby cell, the five servers agree using **Paxos**, a protocol Leslie Lamport described in a paper submitted in 1990 and published, after a long delay, in 1998.[^parliament] Because Paxos is notoriously difficult to understand and implement, Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout at Stanford published **Raft** in 2014, a protocol with the same guarantees designed for clarity. We will use Raft in our diagrams, as the underlying principles are identical.

Both protocols rely on a mathematical property of majorities: out of five servers, any two groups of three share at least one server. If every decision requires the agreement of a majority, two decisions can never be made without at least one server participating in both, and that overlapping server will refuse to approve a second decision that contradicts the first. A network partition cannot create two separate majorities, because there are only five servers in total. The trade-off is availability: a five-server group continues operating while any three servers are running and communicating, tolerates the failure of any two servers, and halts if three fail. A three-server group tolerates one failure. Adding a sixth server does not allow the group to survive more failures, because a majority of six is four, so engineers configure consensus groups with an odd number of servers. Distributed systems engineers evaluate these protocols on two properties: **safety**, the guarantee that the system never makes an invalid decision (such as electing two leaders in one term or committing two different values for the same log entry), and **liveness**, the guarantee that the system eventually makes a decision. Majority-rule protocols preserve safety under all network conditions and sacrifice liveness whenever a majority of servers cannot communicate.

Raft maintains a **replicated log**, an ordered sequence of commands such as "x=2" or "master is server 7" that every server applies in the exact same order. Each log entry records the command alongside the **term** number in which the leader wrote it. Raft divides time into sequential terms numbered 1, 2, 3, and guarantees that at most one leader can be elected in any given term. The leader accepts client writes, appends them to its local log, and sends them to the followers alongside its regular heartbeats. A log entry is **committed** once the leader that created it has replicated it to a majority of servers; servers only apply committed entries to their state and only report committed writes as successful to the client.

When a follower receives no heartbeats during its **election timeout**, a duration of a few hundred milliseconds randomized per server so that followers rarely time out simultaneously, it increments the term number, votes for itself, and requests votes from the other servers. Each server casts at most one vote per term, and votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own.[^uptodate] A candidate that collects votes from a majority of servers becomes the leader for that term and immediately begins sending heartbeats. Any server that receives a message carrying a higher term number than its own immediately steps down to become a follower; the cluster uses term numbers to identify the most recent leader.

blocks.text: We can calculate the latency of these operations directly. Committing a write requires one network round trip from the leader to the nearest majority of servers, plus a synchronous disk write on each participating server before it replies. Within a single datacentre, a network round trip takes less than 1 ms (lesson 1), allowing a consensus group to commit thousands of small writes per second. When servers are distributed across a continent to survive the loss of an entire region, the network round trip takes 30 to 70 ms, adding that latency to every write. If the leader fails, the cluster cannot commit any writes during the election timeout and the subsequent voting round, which takes between a few hundred milliseconds and several seconds.[^flp]

Engineers must handle three operational details when connecting clients to Raft. First, a client finds the leader by querying any server in the group, which returns the address of the current leader, and the client caches that address until a request fails. Second, if a network failure drops the reply to a write request, the client cannot tell whether the write was committed; to prevent duplicate writes on retry, the client attaches a unique ID to every request, and the leader ignores any command whose ID already appears in the log (we will build this mechanism for payment systems in lesson 22). Third, engineers must configure the election timeout to be significantly longer than the heartbeat interval plus a network round trip and disk write, so followers do not trigger unnecessary elections while the leader is healthy, but short enough to recover quickly when the leader crashes; the Raft paper recommends an election timeout of 150 to 300 ms within a single datacentre.
Majority voting prevents the split-brain failure that breaks two-server failover. Before running the next simulation, try to predict which write will survive.

blocks.caption: The same five servers. Partway through, a network partition isolates S1 (the initial leader) and S2 from the other three servers; red crosses mark packets dropped at the partition boundary. Later, the network heals. Predict the outcome, then play the simulation.
blocks.task: Predict which write survives, then play the simulation to the end.

blocks.text: S1 cannot immediately detect that it has been isolated. Remaining the leader of term 1, it accepts the write x=2 from a client and sends the entry to its followers; S2 writes the entry to disk and acknowledges it, while the packets to the other three servers drop. Because two servers out of five do not form a majority, S1 cannot commit x=2, and the client's request hangs. S1 remains a leader but cannot commit new state. On the other side of the partition, S3's election timeout expires; it increments the term to 2, wins votes from S4 and S5 to form a three-server majority, and commits the write x=3 across those three servers. When the network heals, S1 receives a heartbeat from S3 carrying term 2, steps down to become a follower, and overwrites the uncommitted x=2 entry on both its own log and S2's log with the new leader's log. Raft guarantees only that committed entries persist; because x=2 was never committed, the cluster safely discards it.

During the October 2018 outage, GitHub's Orchestrator ran its own leader election using Raft across three sites, and the majority partition promoted the West Coast databases as designed. The failure occurred in the storage layer below Orchestrator. The MySQL primaries on the East Coast did not participate in consensus; they accepted local writes directly and replicated them asynchronously to the West Coast. Although Orchestrator agreed on which database was the new primary, it had no mechanism to stop the isolated East Coast primary from accepting writes during the seconds before it learned it had been demoted, and those writes did not require a majority quorum.

While consensus guarantees that servers agree on who the leader is, acting safely on that leadership requires an additional mechanism, because a deposed leader does not know it has been replaced until it receives a network message, which a network partition can block. Engineers solve this using a **lease**, a mechanism we saw in GFS in lesson 7, which grants a server permission to act as leader for a fixed duration, such as 10 seconds, and must be renewed before it expires. The leader must halt operations the instant its lease expires unless it has successfully renewed it, and the remaining servers guarantee they will not elect a new leader until the old lease has fully expired. In Chubby, the master held a lease granted by the other replicas, and each client maintained a session lease with Chubby lasting about 12 seconds, renewed via keep-alive messages; if a client's session lease expired, Chubby automatically released any locks that client held.[^clocks]

However, time-based leases have a vulnerability that a lock service cannot fix by itself. Suppose a client checks its local clock, verifies that its lease has remaining time, and begins a write operation, but then its process pauses: the language runtime triggers a stop-the-world garbage collection, the hypervisor migrates the virtual machine to another physical host, or the operating system swaps a page of memory to disk. Execution pauses lasting several seconds occur regularly in production. When the process resumes execution, it proceeds directly to the next instruction without rechecking the clock, sending out the write long after its lease has expired.

blocks.text: To prevent stale writes, the storage server must verify the lock's validity on every write. Whenever the lock service grants a lock, it issues a **fencing token**, an integer that increases monotonically with each new lock acquisition (such as the Raft term number or the log index of the lock grant). The client must attach its fencing token to every write request, and the storage system records the highest token number it has processed, rejecting any write carrying a smaller token. When the paused client finally sends its write carrying token 33, the storage server sees that it has already processed token 34 and rejects the request. Chubby implemented this mechanism in 2006 under the name **sequencer**, a byte string containing the lock name and generation number that storage servers could verify; distributed systems researcher Martin Kleppmann introduced the term fencing token in a 2016 analysis of distributed locking. Without fencing tokens, a lock service can elect a new leader, but cannot stop a paused former leader from corrupting storage.

While the core rules of consensus fit on a single page, building a production consensus service requires years of engineering. In 2007, Google engineers Tushar Chandra, Robert Griesemer, and Joshua Redstone published "Paxos Made Live", detailing the work required to turn Lamport's Paxos algorithm into the replicated database underlying Chubby. Most of their engineering effort went into features the theoretical paper omits: handling disks that silently corrupt data, taking snapshots so the replicated log does not grow indefinitely, dynamically reconfiguring group membership, implementing leader leases so the master can serve read requests locally without running a consensus round, and testing a distributed state machine whose bugs surface only under rare combinations of network and hardware failures.

Because consensus protocols are slow and difficult to implement correctly, you should use an existing battle-tested service and restrict it to managing small metadata. Use the consensus service to elect a leader and store configuration records, and let the elected leader process high-volume traffic directly, using its term number as a fencing token. Bigtable never routed table data through Chubby; it used Chubby only to record which tablet server managed which tablet. Later open-source infrastructure copied Chubby's architecture: ZooKeeper, built at Yahoo and published in 2010, served as the coordination service for Hadoop and early versions of Kafka (lesson 16), while etcd, built at CoreOS in 2013 using Raft, stores the cluster state and configuration for Kubernetes.

events.label: No guaranteed agreement with one crash (FLP)

blocks.text: Even a small consensus service becomes something everything depends on. Google's site reliability book tells how Chubby was so dependable that services began to assume it never failed, so its team took it down on purpose, in planned outages, to flush out the services that would break.[^outage] A coordinator that every system relies on deserves the same treatment as GFS's single master in lesson 6: keep it simple, keep it off the data path, and know what happens when it stops.

blocks.caption: Six questions on agreement and leaders
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A primary and a standby database monitor each other with heartbeats, and the standby promotes itself after 10 seconds of silence. What happens when the network link between them fails while both servers remain running?
choices: Nothing harmful: the standby waits 10 seconds, and by then the primary has detected the failure and halted
Both accept writes, because each server concludes the other is dead
Neither accepts writes, because each waits for the other to confirm it is still alive before processing requests
items.why: From the perspective of a remote server, a crashed machine and a machine cut off by a network partition are indistinguishable. With only two servers, neither side can form a majority to break the tie, so both act as primary, causing a split-brain failure.

items.ask: Why do consensus protocols such as Paxos and Raft require a majority of servers to approve every decision?
choices: Any two majorities share at least one server, ensuring the group cannot approve two conflicting decisions
A majority is the minimum number of servers needed to store a complete copy of the log
Majority voting has lower latency than waiting for all servers, and low latency prevents conflicting writes
items.why: Because any two majorities overlap by at least one server, at least one server participates in both decisions and will reject the second if it conflicts with the first. Furthermore, a network partition cannot create two separate majorities.

items.ask: A five-server Raft group is partitioned into one side of two servers (containing the current leader) and another side of three servers. What happens to client writes sent to the isolated old leader?
choices: They are committed on the two-server side and merged into the three-server side when the network heals
They are rejected immediately, because the leader detects the partition from the missing heartbeat replies and steps down
They are never committed because two of five servers is not a majority, and are later overwritten
items.why: The old leader can append the write but not commit it. The side of three elects a new leader in a higher term, and its log replaces the uncommitted entries afterwards.

items.ask: An engineering team needs its consensus group to continue operating when two servers fail simultaneously. What is the smallest group size that meets this requirement, and why?
choices: Four servers, because two failures leave two running servers, which is half of the group
Five servers, because two failures leave three running servers, which forms a majority of five
Three servers, because a single surviving server can still process reads and writes
items.why: A group of n works while a majority is up. Five keeps three after two failures; four needs three of four and so survives only one.

items.ask: A client acquires a lock with a time-bound lease, freezes during a long garbage-collection pause until after the lease expires and a second client acquires the lock, and then resumes execution. What mechanism prevents the first client's delayed write from corrupting storage?
choices: The lease itself: the client's lock library automatically aborts outgoing writes once the local lease timer expires
A shorter lease duration, ensuring the garbage-collection pause lasts longer than the lock grant
A fencing token: the storage server rejects any write carrying a token number lower than the highest token it has already processed
items.why: Because the paused client checked its clock before the pause began, it resumes execution unaware that its lease has expired. Only the storage server, which receives requests from both clients, can compare the monotonically increasing fencing tokens and reject the stale write.

items.ask: Why did Chubby's designers build it for coarse-grained locks held for hours or days, rather than fine-grained locks acquired for each individual request?
choices: Every lock acquisition requires a consensus write round, so lock state changes must be infrequent and kept off the main data path
Long-held locks do not require keep-alive messages, preventing clients from losing locks during short network hiccups
Fine-grained locking requires more than five replicas to scale, and Chubby cells were architecturally limited to five servers
items.why: Consensus costs a majority round trip and a disk write per change. Used to elect a leader that then works alone, it is needed rarely; sessions still use leases and keep-alives whatever the lock's length.

parliament.title: The part-time parliament
parliament.text: Lamport framed his original Paxos paper as an archaeological account of the parliament on the fictional Greek island of Paxos, whose legislators frequently wandered in and out of the chamber. Reviewers found the allegory distracting, delaying the paper's publication for eight years until 1998. In 2001, Lamport published a follow-up paper, "Paxos Made Simple", whose abstract consists of a single sentence: "The Paxos algorithm, when presented in plain English, is very simple."

uptodate.title: At least as up to date
uptodate.text: A log is more up to date if its last entry has a higher term, or the same term and a higher index. Every committed entry is on a majority, and a winning candidate needs votes from a majority, so at least one voter holds each committed entry and refuses a candidate that lacks it. A new leader therefore always has every committed entry. One refinement: an entry left over from an earlier term counts as committed only once an entry of the current term is on a majority, since an old entry on a majority can still be overwritten by a leader that never saw it.

flp.title: Why timeouts are unavoidable
flp.text: In 1985 Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson proved that no protocol can guarantee agreement in a system where messages may take any amount of time and even one server may crash, because a slow server cannot be told from a dead one. Real protocols keep safety always and give up only liveness: with unlucky timing an election can fail and be retried, but two leaders never commit in one term.

clocks.title: Leases and clocks
clocks.text: A lease does not need synchronised clocks, only clocks that run at about the same rate. The holder counts its lease from when it asked, and the grantor from when it answered, which is later, so the holder believes it expires first. A margin for clocks running a little fast or slow covers the rest.

outage.title: Downtime on purpose
outage.text: The story is in "Site Reliability Engineering" (2016). Chubby's global instance was meeting its target so well that other services stopped handling its failures. When it did fail, they failed with it. Its team then took it down for short, planned periods whenever it had run well above its target, so that hidden dependencies showed up in a controlled way.
